lessons.title: മരുന്ന് (marunnŭ) — medicine
lessons.gloss: medicine — the thing that stands between the symptoms you can name and the doctor you can name

segments.text: Say fever. Say a doctor. You have had both for a long while, and nothing at all to put between them.
മരുന്ന് (marunnŭ) — medicine.
You can already name what is wrong — the cough, the pain, the tiredness, the fever — and you can name the person you would go to. മരുന്ന് (marunnŭ) is the thing that was missing in the middle.
This one is not borrowed. It is an old Dravidian word, and Tamil says marundhu for the same thing. The remedy has a native name.

That is worth holding on to, because the next word in this chapter — the one for the treatment itself — came from Sanskrit. The substance is named in Malayalam's own words; the practice is named in borrowed ones.

segments.text: Medicine? (മരുന്ന് (marunnŭ).) Who would you go to for it? (വൈദ്യൻ.) Is this word borrowed? (No — it is Dravidian, and Tamil has it too.)

lessons.title: ചികിത്സ (cikitsa) — treatment
lessons.gloss: treatment — the borrowed word for the practice, beside the native word for the substance

segments.text: Say medicine. Say a doctor. One of those is a thing; the other is a person. Neither is what happens between them.
ചികിത്സ (cikitsa) — treatment.

utterances: ചികിത്സ, cikitsa, what the person does.
മരുന്ന്, marunnŭ, what the person gives.

segments.text: Sanskrit, where the last word was Dravidian. That split is ordinary in Malayalam and you have seen it before: the everyday thing keeps its native name, and the formal practice around it takes a borrowed one.

The Sanskrit word has an unusual shape. Its grammarians build it from a root meaning to perceive, in a form that means wanting to — so the word is put together as something like a wish to see clearly. Treat that as the traditional account rather than a settled fact; what is certain is the borrowing, not the story inside it.

segments.text: Treatment? (ചികിത്സ (cikitsa).) Which of this chapter's two words is borrowed? (ചികിത്സ (cikitsa) — മരുന്ന് (marunnŭ) is Dravidian.) Which one is the substance? (മരുന്ന് (marunnŭ).)

lessons.title: വൃത്തി (vṛtti) — cleanliness
lessons.gloss: cleanliness — a Sanskrit word for how a person conducts themselves, which in Malayalam became how clean a thing is

segments.text: Say medicine, then treatment. Both of those come after something has gone wrong.
വൃത്തി (vṛtti) — cleanliness.

This is the everyday word, and it is worth being plain about its range. It is what you use about a room, a kitchen, a person's hands. Malayalam has a more formal word for hygiene as a subject — the kind printed on a public notice — and this is not it. This is the one people say.
The Sanskrit it comes from does not mean clean at all. vṛtti is conduct — a way of living, how a person carries themselves.

Malayalam narrowed it. The word for how you conduct yourself became the word for how clean you keep things, which is a short step if you have ever been told that keeping a clean house is a matter of character. Take that as the traditional account of the shift rather than a settled fact; the Sanskrit sense and the Malayalam sense are both well attested, and the road between them is the part that is told rather than proved.

segments.instruction: marunnŭ, then vṛtti — the cure, and the thing that comes before needing one

segments.text: Cleanliness? (വൃത്തി (vṛtti).) What did the Sanskrit word behind it mean? (Conduct — a way of living.) Which of this chapter's words is the native one? (മരുന്ന് (marunnŭ).)

lessons.title: വൃത്തി (vṛtti), ചികിത്സ (cikitsa) — on either side of falling ill
lessons.gloss: cleanliness and treatment — one word for keeping well and one for getting well, put on either side of falling ill

segments.text: Say fever. Say cough. Those are the middle of the story.
Lay this chapter out against what you already had and it makes a line:

utterances: പനി, ചുമ, pani, cuma, the thing going wrong.
ചികിത്സ, മരുന്ന്, cikitsa, marunnŭ, after — getting well.

segments.text: You have had the middle of that line for a long while and neither end. You could say what was wrong and name nobody who would help and nothing that would.

lessons.title: (medicine, treatment, cleanliness) (marunnŭ enna ōrmma) — from cold
lessons.gloss: cold retrieval of the three words, and of which one Malayalam did not have to borrow

segments.text: Close the lessons before this one. Say medicine, treatment and cleanliness.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one native word among three

utterances: മരുന്ന്, marunnŭ, Dravidian — Tamil has it too.
വൃത്തി, vṛtti, Sanskrit, and it meant conduct.

segments.text: The thing you swallow kept its own name; the practice and the virtue came in from Sanskrit. That is a pattern, not a coincidence, and you saw the same shape in the school words: the building was assembled at home, the scholarly words arrived whole.

You had the symptoms and the person, and nothing in between. പനി and വേദന came with the other words for feeling unwell, and വൈദ്യൻ came with the words for what people do — so you could say what was wrong and who you would see, and not one word about what would actually be done.
Now the line runs end to end: keep clean, fall ill, be treated, take the medicine.
